title: Plant Hormones: Gibberellins
objective: Explain gibberellin control of elongation, germination, developmental transitions, and reproductive traits while separating endogenous signaling from chemical treatment claims.

terms.definition: Diterpenoid growth-regulator family involved in germination, elongation, and developmental transitions.
Growth-repressing regulatory protein degraded after active gibberellin signaling.
Rapid stem elongation associated with transition toward reproduction in some plant forms.
Stem segment between two nodes whose length reflects cell division and elongation.

coreScience: Gibberellins regulate seed reserve mobilization, stem and internode elongation, leaf expansion, flowering-related processes, and reproductive development. Active gibberellin signaling promotes degradation of DELLA repressors, releasing growth programs. The outcome depends on which gibberellin is active, where it is produced, tissue sensitivity, and interactions with light and other hormones.

Internode length is not a gibberellin measurement. Spectrum, daily light, temperature, plant density, root restriction, nitrogen, water, genetics, and developmental stage also affect elongation. Compact plants can differ in gibberellin synthesis, deactivation, transport, perception, or completely separate pathways.

Historical and modern cannabis observations link hormone treatments with sex expression and architecture, but chemical response is not a safe shortcut to infer natural sex biology. Concentration, developmental window, genotype, formulation, worker exposure, residues, and legal status all matter.
cultivationRelevance: Track node number and internode length separately. Height gain can come from added nodes, longer internodes, or both.
Do not use unregistered growth regulators to control stretch or sex expression. Production actions are governed by labels, worker safety, residue rules, and jurisdiction.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Height, node count, individual internode lengths, branch angles, and growth interval.
Age, photoperiod, preflower/flower stage, sex-expression observations, and transition date.
Day/night and leaf temperature, DLI, spectrum, density, root volume, water, and N status.
Regulator identity, concentration, formulation, label/legal status, exposure, and controls.
Elongation, flower timing, abnormalities, residues if tested, and follow-up generations where relevant.

misconceptions: Stretch proves excess gibberellin: Many environmental and genetic factors alter internode length.
Gibberellins only affect height: They also participate in germination and reproductive development.
A sex-expression treatment rewrites genotype: It alters developmental expression under specific conditions; genetic identity remains a separate question.
evidenceLimits: Cannabis hormone-treatment literature spans differing plant types and older methods. Do not translate historical experimental doses into present cultivation instructions.
